c:clock_add_jump_callback.why: time-jump notification -- rcl calls back when the clock steps (simulation reset, NTP correction), with a threshold selecting which jumps qualify. Ours has no notification at all; on a device a monotonic clock does not step, and the simulation case now has ROS time in every language (issue 0789) without anyone asking to be TOLD that the clock stepped -- a simulator writes the time, the nodes read it.

Describes which KIND of change occurred (ROS time activated, deactivated, stepped).

c:clock_get_now_ns.why: rcl's `rcl_clock_get_now(clock, rcl_time_point_value_t* out)` writes through a pointer and returns a status. Ours returns the nanoseconds directly, because a clock read cannot fail once the clock is valid -- the platform seam (RFC-0073) either has a clock or the image did not boot.

The row reports ours-only because the two projects spell one predicate differently, not because the capability is ours alone. This is the ours-only half of `c:clock_valid`; both halves now make the same statement from their own side. No code change.

c:clock_valid.why:
RE-VERDICTED rename -> their-rename 2026-09-05 (phase-425). The row already contained its own refutation: it recorded that rcl is the inconsistent one and then filed the work under `rename`, which by `_doc` means OURS is the name that should change. Nothing on our side should move -- `nros_clock_is_valid` is the shape rcl uses fourteen other times. The trailing clause "the drop-in claim is about matching, not about being right" is the DROP-IN COST, which `their-rename` records rather than cancels: a ported rcl node still rewrites `rcl_clock_valid(&c)` as `nros_clock_is_valid(&c)`. What it stops doing is sitting on the campaign's work list, where it would have inverted our predicate naming to chase rcl's one exception. Pair: `c:clock_is_valid`. No code change.

c:difference_times.why: rcl's `rcl_difference_times(const rcl_time_point_t *start, const rcl_time_point_t *finish, rcl_duration_t *delta)` -- **Time - Time -> Duration** (`docs/reference/api-surface/rclc.json`). CORRECTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5, group B): the previous text read "Same operation", pairing this with `nros_time_sub` on the grounds that `sub` matches `nros_time_add`. It is NOT the same operation. `nros_time_sub(nros_time_t time, nros_duration_t duration) -> nros_time_t` (`packages/api/nros-c/src/clock.rs:530`, `nros_generated.h:3130`) is **Time - Duration -> Time** -- different operands, different return type, different meaning. Renaming it would have put rcl's name on a function that computes something else, which is why the row could argue for our spelling and call itself a rename at the same time: there was never a rename to make. Contrast `c:clock_valid`, where the operation IS identical and only the spelling differs, so `the drop-in claim is about matching, not about being right` decides it. That clause is absent here because it does not apply. So this is a theirs-only operation our C does not ship at all: a gap. And it is the `our languages disagree` shape of issues 0788 / 0789 rather than a naming question -- C++ ships it as `Time::operator-(const Time&) -> Duration` (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/time.hpp:85`) and Rust as `impl Sub<Time> for Time { type Output = Duration }` (`packages/core/nros-core/src/time.rs:118`); only C has no way to get a duration out of two timestamps. No target name is proposed: filling a gap is an ADDITION, and what to call the addition is the addition's decision, not this row's.

rename.resolution: RE-VERDICTED rename -> gap. The two functions are different operations (Time-Time->Duration vs Time-Duration->Time), so the rename premise was false and no target name is needed. C lacks the operation that C++ (time.hpp:85) and Rust (time.rs:118) both ship.

c:duration_from_nanoseconds.why: the duration half of `c:time_from_nanoseconds` -- the same `{sec, nanosec}` split, on `nros_duration_t`. rcl's duration is a bare signed nanosecond count (`c:duration_value_t`) so it needs no constructor; ours is the wire struct, and a SIGNED span has to floor rather than truncate (issue 0799). Its absence is what made the C++ `Duration::to_msg` open-code the split.

c:duration_value_t.why: rcl's duration is a distinct signed nanosecond type. Ours are `uint64_t` milliseconds at the C API's timer entry points and a `TimerDuration` in Rust -- the unit is named in the parameter rather than in a typedef. This is why the QoS accessors read `deadline_ms` rather than `deadline`; see the qos stage.

c:executor_add_time_triggered_dispatcher.why: registers a time-triggered dispatcher -- the fixed-schedule execution shape RFC-0078/0079 need for a WCET-declared tier. rclc's executor has a `rclc_executor_set_trigger` hook but no schedule; ROS 2 has no counterpart at all.

c:get_ros_time_override.why: reads the installed ROS time back. rcl has no such entry point -- a caller there reads the clock -- but our Rust `Clock` has `get_ros_time_override`, and issue 0789 is about the two languages having the same switches. Returns `NROS_RET_NOT_FOUND` when no override is in effect, which is the `Option` the Rust one returns.

ROS 2 reaches the same thing through rcutils and an OS that always has one; a bare-metal target may have only a cycle counter. Not application API -- see issue 0784 for the same complaint about seams reaching `nros::`.

c:ros_clock_fini.why: rcl builds a clock per kind through a named init pair (`rcl_steady_clock_init`, `rcl_system_clock_init`, `rcl_ros_clock_init`) as well as a generic `rcl_clock_init` taking a `rcl_clock_type_t`. Ours is the generic form only -- `nros_clock_init(clock, type)` -- because a per-kind entry point buys nothing when the kinds are an enum, and the allocator argument they also carry does not exist.

c:sleep_ms.why: rclcpp's `Rate` blocks the calling thread in a sleep loop to hold a fixed frequency. RFC-0021 forbids a blocking helper that does not drive the executor -- a `Rate::sleep` on a single-threaded executor stops the transport for the whole period. The periodic work shape here is a timer, which the executor drives. rclc's `rclc_sleep_ms` is the same shape. Our platform sleep (`nros_platform_sleep_us`) exists for the BOARD layer, not for application code.

c:time_add.why: `nros_time_add(nros_time_t, nros_duration_t) -> nros_time_t`. rcl has no time addition at all. CORRECTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5, group B): the old text offered `only rcl_difference_times` as the neighbouring operation, which reads as though the two were a pair; they are not -- `rcl_difference_times` is Time - Time -> Duration and has no additive form. Ours pairs with `nros_time_sub` (Time +/- Duration -> Time), matching C++ (time.hpp:78/81) and Rust (time.rs:100/109). See `c:difference_times`.

c:time_sub.why: `nros_time_sub(nros_time_t, nros_duration_t) -> nros_time_t` -- subtract a DURATION from a TIME. CORRECTED 2026-08-26 (phase-379 W5, group B): this is NOT `the ours-only half of c:difference_times`. rcl's function is Time - Time -> Duration; this one is Time - Duration -> Time, and rcl has no Time - Duration operation under any spelling. Ours is the extension because C++ (`Time::operator-(const Duration&)`, time.hpp:81) and Rust (`impl Sub<Duration> for Time`, time.rs:109) both ship it and C agrees with them.

c:timer_call.why: rclcpp's internal dispatch entry point; a user writes neither side. See the pubsub stage.

c:timer_clock.why: reads back the clock a timer was created against. Ours are created on the executor's clock and cannot be created on another, so the accessor would return a constant.

c:timer_exchange_callback.why: swaps a timer's callback at runtime. The callback is bound to the ENTITY at creation (RFC-0041) so the executor's static dispatch table cannot be rewritten while it is being walked.

c:timer_exchange_period.why: changes a timer's period at runtime. Rust has `Timer::set_oneshot`/`set_repeating`/`set_inert` but no period change either -- a node whose rate is a parameter has to destroy and recreate the timer. Phase 379 W3.

c:timer_get_allocator.why: one global allocator; see the `no-allocator` rule.

c:timer_get_callback.why: reads back the callback pointer. Ours is bound at creation and not swappable; see `c:timer_exchange_callback`.

c:timer_get_guard_condition.why: the guard condition rcl fires to wake a wait set when a timer is reset. RFC-0002's executor recomputes its next deadline directly (`next_deadline_ms`); there is no wait set to interrupt.

c:timer_get_next_call_time.why: when this timer next fires. Rust has it (`Timer::time_until_next_call`) and C does not. Phase 379 W3.

c:timer_get_period.why: rcl writes the period through an `int64_t*` and returns a status; ours returns it. Same inversion as `c:clock_get_now_ns`, and the same reason: reading a valid timer's own period cannot fail. This is one of the eight C rows the first report could not explain, and it is explained by the same decision as the clock read rather than by anything specific to timers.

c:timer_get_time_since_last_call.why: Rust has `Timer::time_since_last_call`; C does not. See `c:timer_get_next_call_time`.

c:timer_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl; our handles carry their state inline. See `c:publisher_impl_t`.

c:timer_init_default.why: rclc's default wrapper; `nros_timer_init` IS the default form. See `c:publisher_init_default`.

c:timer_is_canceled.why: our C timer has no cancel predicate at all -- neither spelling. C++ and Rust both have one. Phase 379 W3.

c:timer_is_ready.why: Rust has `Timer::is_ready`; C does not. See `c:timer_get_next_call_time`.

cpp:ClockQoS::ClockQoS.why: rclcpp gives each QoS preset its own type; ours are named constructors on one `QoS` -- but C++ ships only THREE (`default_profile`, `sensor_data`, `services`, qos.hpp:175-181) and no clock preset under any name, while our Rust `QoSProfile` has twelve including `clock_default`. So this is not the preset-as-a-type divergence recorded for `cpp:ServicesQoS::ServicesQoS`; it is a preset our own Rust publishes the clock on and our C++ cannot spell. The qos stage owns the family. Phase 379 W3. COLLAPSE CHECK 2026-09-04 (phase-417): the preset now ships as a type on the ported surface (`rclcpp::ClockQoS`, phase-417 W3.f, ADOPT), so this correlates `same` there. The row survives because `--check` gates the NATIVE bucket, where this is still `theirs-only`: `nros::QoS` still has no clock preset. See `cpp:ClockQoS`.

cpp:ComponentNode::create_wall_timer.why:
rclcpp's `Node::create_wall_timer(period, callback)` on the RFC-0044 base: ours is `create_wall_timer<Self, &Self::tick>(period_ms)`, the member bound at compile time for the reason `cpp:ComponentNode::create_subscription` gives, plus a `(period_ms, nros_cpp_timer_callback_t, void* ctx)` escape hatch for non-member handlers. The NAME half of the pair is already recorded: `cpp:Node::create_wall_timer` (rename -- ours should carry rclcpp's name) and `cpp:Node::create_timer` (its ours-only half); this row is that same pair one type over, and the type name is the additional question (`cpp:ComponentNode`). RENAMED 2026-09-05 (phase-425 W1) with the base: both overloads are thin wrappers over `Node::create_wall_timer`, so they moved with it, as did the macro (`NROS_CREATE_WALL_TIMER`). `create_timer_in` keeps its stem. The type name `ComponentNode` remains the additional, separate question.

rust:TimerClock.why:
RE-VERDICTED declined -> divergence 2026-09-05 (phase-425 W4/W5). The row's reason has stopped being true, and it was the whole of the verdict: it said "our timers are created on the executor's clock and cannot be created on another", and there is now `Executor::register_timer_on_clock(period, TimerClockSource, cb)`. A per-timer clock selector exists.

`TimerClock` is rclrs's version of it — an enum of `SteadyTime` / `SystemTime` / `NodeTime` / `Clock(&Clock)` (`rclrs/src/timer/timer_options.rs`), reached through `IntoTimerOptions`. Ours is `rust:TimerClockSource`, three variants, on a second registrar rather than an options builder.

The CONSTRAINT is what collapses their four variants into three: the ROS-time override is process-global — one simulated clock per image, which is the model `nros_core::Clock` documents and the model `/clock` itself has — so there is no per-timer `Clock` object to borrow and no separate NODE clock to distinguish from it. `Clock(&Clock)` and `NodeTime` are one thing here, and that thing is `Ros`.

The `IntoTimerOptions` family stays `declined` on its own terms: the options BUILDER is a shape question (a fluent per-site options object against a named registrar), separate from whether the capability exists.

rust:TimerClockSource.why:
phase-425 W4. Which clock advances a timer: `Steady` (the default and every pre-existing timer — it consumes the spin delta the executor already measured, so it costs nothing), `Ros` (`/clock` when a source is active, system time when none is — the same fallback `rclcpp::Clock` has), and `System`.

rclrs's counterpart is `rust:TimerClock`, and the differences are both constraint-driven. THREE variants and not four, because the ROS-time override is process-global — one simulated clock per image — so there is no per-timer `Clock` object to borrow and no node clock distinct from it; rclrs's `Clock(&Clock)` and `NodeTime` are one variant here. And a SECOND REGISTRAR rather than a field on an options builder, because a non-`Steady` timer reads its clock on every poll: on a target that is a platform call, and the cost belongs at the call site rather than behind a default.

Re-exported from `nros` and not only `nros-node`: 62 of the 62 in-workspace dep-sites depend on the umbrella, so a type that stops at the core crate is one no application can name. W4 stopped at the core, which is what the `/clock` fixture found the moment it tried to write a timer.

rust:TimerClock::is_node_time.why: **rclrs 0.7.0 CONVERGED ON OUR SHAPE.** 0.5.1 had one `create_timer`; 0.7.0 has `create_timer_inert` / `create_timer_oneshot` / `create_timer_repeating` -- the same three modes our `TimerMode` carries, arrived at independently. Ours are a mode SET ON an entity in the static table (`set_inert`, `set_oneshot`, `set_repeating`) because a static table cannot grow a timer at runtime and re-arming is how a one-shot is reused; rclrs constructs one per mode. Same model, different placement -- so this is no longer the divergence the 0.5.1 comparison recorded, and W5 should consider matching the verb.

rust:TimerDuration.why: `TimerDuration` is the unit a timer period is expressed in and `Duration` is the ROS message duration; rclrs has one `Duration` (a re-export of `std::time::Duration` shape) for both.
